newsitem.title: UK: Politics turn upside down in British campaign.
newsitem.headline: Politics turn upside down in British campaign.

text.p: In the topsy-turvy world of British politics, it was the opposition Labour Party that radiated authority on Thursday while the Conservatives, in power for 18 years, wooed voters with pledges of change.

As the main parties set out their policy stalls for a May 1 general election, voters could finally see just how much has been turned on its head since "old Labour" became "new Labour" and the Conservatives' iron grip on Britain melted away.

Former prime minister Margaret Thatcher, who turned Labour and socialism into dirty political words during the tumultuous 1980s, has even been quoted as saying Britain would now be safe with Labour: heresy to her Conservative colleagues.
Yet some in her party quietly say the "Iron Lady" was right and think it time for the Conservatives to head for the wilderness and take stock.

For in the Alice-in-Wonderland landscape of 1997, it is Labour that looks safe and the Conservatives who flail and fight each other at every turn of a campaign for an election that they are widely expected to lose.
How things change.
As Labour leader Tony Blair unveiled his party's manifesto on Thursday, one key word surfaced time and again -- the "T" word that has helped lose Labour so many elections.
"This election is about trust," Blair said at the launch, a slick, one-man show packaged up with pop music and far removed from the stolid party platforms of old.

"Trust is the single most important commodity in this election and I know why, I mean I can almost reach out and feel that sentiment amongst the public. They want a new beginning in politics but they want to know they can trust the person who is offering them that," Blair said.
He radiated confidence, calm, stability and authority -- not bad for a man of 43 who has never held government office.
Blair promised low inflation, tough crime policies, support for enterprise: in short, what the Conservatives already offer.
"I'm not going to stand here and tell you that everything in the last 18 years has been a disaster. There are some things the Conservatives got right," he said.
Yet it is the trusty old Conservatives who now struggle to win voters' confidence, mired in sex and sleaze scandals and taunted daily over broken tax pledges.
Never mind that the British economy is in good shape -- the people of Britain don't want to give the government credit.

"Honest John" Major, who defied the polls to win the last election with a majority of 21 in 1992 and is hoping for a re-run this time around, faced repeated questions about his party's trustworthiness when he unveiled the Conservatives' manifesto on Wednesday.
Time and again, reporters demanded to know how Major's plan for tax breaks would add up and how on earth the Conservatives could run for a record fifth consecutive term on a platform of change.
"It is time for a change," Major insisted. "Time for a change to the next phase of Conservative prosperity."
Yet no sooner had he unveiled the manifesto than Labour derired his plans for the economy as "reckless and desperate".
Nobody winced at the clear reversal in roles.
Blair accused Major of "spraying around tax promises" that could not be kept if the economy was to prosper.
Not an eyebrow was raised.
He said the Conservatives had run "boom and bust economies" -- once seen as Labour's claim to fame -- and that Labour could now steer a better course "without regard to dogma or doctrine".
Even the financial markets, which once dreaded the prospect of a Labour victory, have turned tail in this upside-down campaign and see little to fear from life under Blair.
"The market didn't appear to pay any attention to the Labour manifesto at all. On paper, the two parties have very similar policies," said Royal Bank of Scotland economist Marian Bell.
